citation: Temporal Technologies, State of Development 2026, temporal.io/reports/state-of-development-2026, published 25 August 2026 (page 'About the Report' date). No named authors.
source_tier: Company research (vendor-commissioned survey run by Qualtrics)
access_status: Fully read via web fetch of the live page (text extracted by a fetch tool, not a PDF; charts not seen, only their text). Re-opened this session.

The report's blockers (state tracking, debugging) map onto what Temporal sells. Temporal's own use of 'not correlated' for agent count versus issues does not obviously serve the pitch, but the survey is not independent.

date_and_recency: Published 25 August 2026. Data collected 29 April to 25 May 2026 (Qualtrics).
key_claims: Respondents run a median of 5.0 agents but a mean of 10.7, so a minority run many. Agent count and frequency of issues are not correlated (stated without a coefficient or test on the page text). 41.1% hit issues with agents daily or more. Leadership roles are more likely than engineers to call their organization 'very successful' (43.7% vs 32.4%).
headline_figures: Median 5.0 agents per respondent; mean 10.7 (Chart 1.5, self-reported, unit is respondent). 41.1% encounter issues daily or more (Chart 2.6). 43.7% of CEOs/management/VPs/directors vs 32.4% of others (engineers) say organization 'very successful' (Chart 2.5); the page words this as '1.4x' in the body and '35.1% more likely' in the callout, and 43.7/32.4 is about 1.35, so the two wordings are close but not the same. n=554.
sample_unit_and_population: 554 retained respondents after removing low-quality responses; about two-thirds US, one third UK/EMEA. Mostly engineers with 6-15 years of coding experience (58.9%). Roles: engineer/AI engineer 25.6%, VP/director of IT 13.9%, data engineer 11.9%, plus DevOps/platform engineer, architect, data scientist, CEO/management. Software engineers are a large part but not all. Note 'leader' group here is CEO, management, VP and director combined.
observed_vs_stated: Stated. Agent counts, issue frequency and organizational success are all self-reported; success is explicitly self-reported.
what_makes_oversight_tiring: [uncertain] The page gives no mechanism for oversight fatigue. Closest: manual checking is the only certain way to know an agent did its job beyond time-consuming testing and proofs; engineers cite lack of time to think as a bottleneck; some worry leadership will keep raising expectations. These are not framed as supervision load.
consequence_for_quality: Not addressed as a load effect. The page says 41.1% hit issues daily or more, and that issue frequency is not correlated with number of agents. It reports nothing on missed defects, errors from fatigue or retention.
what_reduces_the_load: Not addressed directly. The vendor's pitch is orchestration with durable state and human-intervention triggers; the page text read does not claim this reduces supervision effort. A free-text comment says trust holds 'as long as humans remain responsible for validation' (from earlier read, not re-quoted this session).
limitations_stated: 'Each team may define issues differently, issues can range in severity,' and 'those who pay closer attention will notice more of the granular issues.' 'When we discuss those who are "successful at using AI agents," that is self-reported data.' Low-quality responses removed (554 retained).
counter_evidence: Vendor survey, self-report only. Mean (10.7) far above median (5.0) implies a skewed distribution, but no distribution, definition-of-agent consistency check or correlation statistic is shown in the text read, so 'not correlated' is an unsupported-by-detail assertion. No data on oversight burden, so this source cannot support a cognitive-load claim. Leader vs engineer gap is perception, not outcome, and not causal.
verification_status: Checked against the live page opened this session: median 5.0 and mean 10.7; 'not correlated' sentence; 43.7% vs 32.4%; role mix; publication and survey dates; limitations. Confirmed absent from the page text: any mention of review load, supervision time, fatigue or burnout (as reported by the fetch tool, which summarises; a full-page keyword check was not independently run) [uncertain].
usable_claim: In a Temporal-commissioned survey of 554 US and UK respondents (29 April to 25 May 2026), the median respondent reported using 5 agents and the mean was 10.7. Temporal says the number of agents and the frequency of issues were not correlated. Leadership roles were more likely than others to call their organization very successful with agents (43.7% vs 32.4%, self-reported).
do_not_use: Do not use this report as evidence of oversight fatigue, review load or supervision time: it says nothing on them. Do not say agent count has no effect on workload (only issue frequency was reported uncorrelated). Do not call 43.7 vs 32.4 a measured success gap; it is self-reported perception. Do not use '1.4x' and '35.1%' interchangeably. Do not present as independent research.
overlap_with_existing_essays: The trust essay already draws on this report (85.5% trust, 41.1% daily issues). The agents-per-person, not-correlated and leader-vs-engineer figures are new to it. Not checked against Verification Gap or Checking Isn't Catching [uncertain].
